about: Chemistry 1 (CENG40006) is a compulsory 7.5-credit Spring-term module in Year 1 of Imperial's MEng Chemical Engineering (2026-27 programme specification). Imperial publishes no syllabus or description for it, only the title, so the topics here are a generic first-year 'chemistry for chemical engineers' set chosen by us, not Imperial's list: atomic structure and bonding, stoichiometry, acid–base and redox chemistry, transition-metal chemistry and organic chemistry. Year 1 also has a separate Autumn-term Physical Chemistry module (CENG40008), so some of this material (for example atomic structure, bonding or electrochemistry) may be taught there instead; check the topics against your lecture list. No module-level assessment details are published.
topics: Chemical bonding, molecular shape and intermolecular forces
Organic structure, functional groups and isomerism

notes.h: Atomic structure, electron configuration and periodic trends
notes.body:
Chemical behaviour, from bond strength to catalyst activity, follows from how electrons are arranged in atoms. This topic revisits A-level ideas with more quantum detail.

Atomic orbitals and quantum numbers
- Principal quantum number n (1, 2, 3…): shell and main energy level.
- Angular momentum quantum number l (0 to n − 1): subshell shape; l = 0, 1, 2, 3 are s, p, d, f.
- Magnetic quantum number m_l (−l to +l): orientation; so there are 1 s, 3 p, 5 d and 7 f orbitals per subshell.
- Spin quantum number m_s = +½ or −½.

Filling rules
- Aufbau principle: fill lowest-energy orbitals first (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p…).
- Pauli exclusion principle: no two electrons in an atom share all four quantum numbers, so each orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin.
- Hund's rule: electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly, with parallel spins, before pairing.
- Exceptions: Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ and Cu is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ (half-filled and filled d subshells are especially stable).
- In transition-metal ions, 4s electrons are lost before 3d: Fe is [Ar]3d⁶4s², Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶, Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵.

Atomic spectra
The hydrogen atom has energy levels Eₙ = −13.6 eV/n². A transition from n = 2 to n = 1 emits 13.6 × (1 − ¼) = 10.2 eV, a photon of wavelength λ = hc/E ≈ 122 nm (ultraviolet). The n = 3 to n = 2 transition gives about 656 nm (red). Line spectra are the evidence for quantised energy levels.

Periodic trends
- Effective nuclear charge (Z_eff) increases across a period because extra protons are only partly shielded by electrons in the same shell.
- Atomic radius: decreases across a period (higher Z_eff), increases down a group (more shells).
- First ionisation energy: generally increases across a period and decreases down a group. Two classic dips in period 2: B is lower than Be (the 2p electron is higher in energy and shielded by 2s), and O is lower than N (the paired electron in a 2p orbital is repelled by its partner).
- Electronegativity (Pauling scale): increases across a period and up a group; F is the highest at about 4.0, then O (about 3.4), with N and Cl both about 3.0–3.2.
- Metallic character increases down a group and to the left.

Why this matters to chemical engineers
- Electronegativity differences predict bond polarity, which controls solubility and separation behaviour.
- Ionisation energies and configurations explain why transition metals have variable oxidation states and act as catalysts.

Exam tips: write configurations in full or with noble-gas cores, remember the Cr and Cu exceptions, and explain trends in terms of nuclear charge, shielding and distance.

notes.h: Bonding, molecular shape and intermolecular forces
notes.body:
The type of bonding and the shape of a molecule decide its polarity, and polarity and intermolecular forces decide boiling points, solubility and how substances can be separated, which is central to chemical engineering.

Types of bonding
- Ionic: electron transfer between atoms with a large electronegativity difference (e.g. NaCl); a giant lattice held by electrostatic attraction; high melting points, conducts when molten or dissolved.
- Covalent: shared electron pairs; can be non-polar (equal sharing) or polar (unequal sharing when electronegativities differ).
- Metallic: positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons; good electrical and thermal conductivity.

Lewis structures and VSEPR
Valence-shell electron-pair repulsion: electron pairs (bonding and lone) around a central atom arrange themselves as far apart as possible. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs.
- 2 pairs: linear, 180° (CO₂, BeCl₂)
- 3 pairs: trigonal planar, 120° (BF₃)
- 4 pairs: tetrahedral, 109.5° (CH₄); with one lone pair, trigonal pyramidal, about 107° (NH₃); with two lone pairs, bent, about 104.5° (H₂O)
- 5 pairs: trigonal bipyramidal (PCl₅)
- 6 pairs: octahedral, 90° (SF₆)

Hybridisation and multiple bonds
- sp³ (tetrahedral), sp² (trigonal planar), sp (linear).
- A double bond is one σ bond plus one π bond (e.g. ethene, sp² carbons); a triple bond is one σ plus two π bonds (ethyne, sp carbons). π bonds stop rotation, giving rise to E/Z isomerism.

Polarity
A molecule is polar if it has polar bonds arranged so their dipoles do not cancel. CO₂ has polar C=O bonds but is linear, so it is non-polar; H₂O is bent, so it is polar.

Intermolecular forces (weakest to strongest, typically)
- London (dispersion) forces: temporary induced dipoles; present in all molecules; increase with the number of electrons and surface area.
- Permanent dipole–dipole forces between polar molecules.
- Hydrogen bonds: H bonded to N, O or F interacting with a lone pair on another N, O or F. This is why water boils at 100 °C while H₂S, a heavier molecule, boils at about −60 °C.

Bond enthalpies
Mean bond enthalpies give rough reaction enthalpies: ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
Example using typical mean values (C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O in CO₂ 805, O–H 464 kJ/mol) for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O(g): broken 2648, formed 3466, so ΔH ≈ −818 kJ/mol. The measured value for gaseous water is about −802 kJ/mol; the gap shows that mean values are averages over many compounds.

Exam tips: draw the Lewis structure first, count electron pairs, then name the shape (based on atoms, not lone pairs) and judge polarity from symmetry.

notes.h: Stoichiometry: moles, limiting reactants, conversion and yield
notes.body:
Stoichiometry is the bookkeeping of chemistry. Chemical engineers use it constantly: to size feeds, to work out how much product a reactor makes, and to write material balances.

Moles and balanced equations
- Amount n (mol) = mass/molar mass. Engineers often work in kmol and kg, or in molar flow rates (mol/s).
- A balanced equation gives mole ratios, not mass ratios. For example CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O: 1 mol methane needs 2 mol oxygen. In mass terms, 100 kg of CH₄ (6.23 kmol) needs about 399 kg of O₂.
- Ideal gas: pV = nRT. At 0 °C and 1 atm a mole of ideal gas occupies about 22.4 L; at 25 °C and 1 bar, about 24.8 L.
- Concentration c = n/V (mol/dm³, written M).

Empirical and molecular formula
Divide each mass percentage by the atomic mass and scale to the smallest ratio. Example: 40.0% C, 6.7% H, 53.3% O gives a ratio of about 1 : 2 : 1, so CH₂O. If the molar mass is 180 g/mol, the molecular formula is C₆H₁₂O₆.

Limiting and excess reactants
- The limiting reactant runs out first and sets the maximum product.
- Percentage excess = (amount fed − amount needed to react with the limiting reactant)/(amount needed) × 100.
Example: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ with 28 kg N₂ (1.00 kmol) and 8 kg H₂ (3.97 kmol). The N₂ needs 3.00 kmol H₂, so N₂ is limiting and H₂ is in about 32% excess. Maximum NH₃ = 2.00 kmol ≈ 34.0 kg.

Engineering measures of reaction performance
- Fractional conversion of a reactant X = (moles reacted)/(moles fed).
- Yield: commonly, moles of desired product formed divided by the moles that would have formed if all the limiting reactant had reacted to it with no side reactions. If 25 kg of NH₃ is actually obtained in the example, the yield is 25/34.0 ≈ 73%.
- Selectivity: moles of desired product formed per mole of undesired product (or per mole of reactant consumed). Definitions vary between textbooks, so always state the one you use.

Combustion terms
- Theoretical oxygen: the O₂ needed for complete combustion of all the fuel to CO₂ and H₂O.
- Theoretical air: the air that contains that oxygen (air is about 21% O₂ and 79% N₂ by moles).
- Excess air is based on theoretical air, even if combustion is incomplete.
- Flue gas analysis may be given on a wet basis or a dry basis (water removed).

Extent of reaction
For a single reaction, nᵢ = nᵢ,₀ + νᵢξ, where νᵢ is the stoichiometric coefficient (negative for reactants) and ξ the extent of reaction. This keeps balances consistent when several species change.

Exam tips: always convert to moles first, identify the limiting reactant explicitly, and state definitions of yield and selectivity before using them.

Acid–base chemistry matters in process chemistry, effluent treatment, corrosion and biochemical engineering. Most of it rests on equilibrium constants.

Definitions
- Brønsted–Lowry: an acid is a proton (H⁺) donor and a base is a proton acceptor. Every acid has a conjugate base: CH₃COOH/CH₃COO⁻, NH₄⁺/NH₃.
- Lewis: an acid is an electron-pair acceptor and a base an electron-pair donor (e.g. BF₃ accepting the lone pair on NH₃). This includes reactions with no proton transfer.

pH and water
- pH = −log₁₀[H₃O⁺].
- Water self-ionises: Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C, so pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C.
- Kw rises with temperature, so neutral pH is 7 only at 25 °C; at higher temperatures neutral water has pH below 7 but is still neutral ([H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻]).

Strong and weak acids and bases
- Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄ first proton) ionise essentially completely: 0.010 M HCl has pH 2.0.
- Strong bases (NaOH): 0.0010 M NaOH has pOH 3, so pH 11 at 25 °C.
- Weak acids partly ionise: Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA], pKa = −log Ka. A smaller pKa means a stronger acid.
- For a weak acid that ionises only slightly, [H₃O⁺] ≈ √(Ka c).
- For a conjugate pair, Ka × Kb = Kw, so pKa + pKb = 14 at 25 °C.

Worked example: 0.10 M ethanoic (acetic) acid, pKa ≈ 4.76 (Ka ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁵)
- [H₃O⁺] ≈ √(1.74 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.10) ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻³ M, so pH ≈ 2.88.
- Check: only about 1.3% is ionised, so the approximation is fine.

Buffers
- A buffer is a mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid) that resists pH change when small amounts of acid or base are added.
- Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log₁₀([A⁻]/[HA]).
- Example: 0.10 M ethanoic acid with 0.20 M sodium ethanoate gives pH ≈ 4.76 + log 2 ≈ 5.06.
- Buffers work best within about ±1 pH unit of the pKa, and capacity increases with concentration.

Titrations
- Strong acid with strong base: equivalence at pH 7 (at 25 °C), with a steep jump.
- Weak acid with strong base: equivalence pH above 7 (the conjugate base is basic). At half-equivalence, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa, a practical way to measure pKa.
- Choose an indicator whose colour change range lies on the steep part of the curve (phenolphthalein, about pH 8.2–10, for weak acid with strong base).

Exam tips: write the equilibrium expression, state any approximation and check it, and keep track of whether you have found pH or pOH.

Redox reactions drive batteries, fuel cells, electrolysis (chlor-alkali, aluminium smelting, electroplating, electrorefining) and corrosion, all of which chemical engineers design or fight.

Oxidation and reduction
- Oxidation is loss of electrons (increase in oxidation state); reduction is gain of electrons (decrease in oxidation state).
- Oxidation state rules: elements are 0; O is usually −2 (−1 in peroxides); H is usually +1; the sum equals the overall charge. Examples: Mn in MnO₄⁻ is +7; Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻ is +6.

Balancing redox equations in acid
1. Write the two half-equations.
2. Balance atoms other than O and H.
3. Balance O with H₂O, then H with H⁺.
4. Balance charge with electrons.
5. Multiply so electrons cancel, then add.
Example: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O and Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ combine to MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O.

Electrochemical cells
- Galvanic (voltaic) cell: a spontaneous reaction produces electricity. Oxidation at the anode (negative), reduction at the cathode (positive).
- Standard electrode potentials E° are measured against the standard hydrogen electrode (0 V) at 298 K, 1 bar and 1 mol/dm³.
- E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode), using reduction potentials for both.
- Daniell cell: Cu²⁺/Cu is +0.34 V and Zn²⁺/Zn is −0.76 V, so E°cell = 1.10 V.
- Thermodynamic link: ΔG° = −nFE°cell, with F = 96 485 C/mol. For the Daniell cell (n = 2), ΔG° ≈ −212 kJ/mol. A positive E°cell means the reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions.
- Also ΔG° = −RT ln K, so a large E° means a very large equilibrium constant.

Nernst equation
E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q, which at 298 K is E = E° − (0.0592/n) log₁₀ Q.
Example: a Daniell cell with [Zn²⁺] = 1.0 M and [Cu²⁺] = 0.010 M has Q = 100, so E = 1.10 − (0.0592/2) × 2 ≈ 1.04 V.

Electrolysis
- An external voltage drives a non-spontaneous reaction. Oxidation still happens at the anode, which is now positive.
- Faraday's laws: charge Q = It, moles of electrons = Q/F. Example: 10 A for 1 hour passes 36 000 C = 0.373 mol of electrons, depositing 0.187 mol Cu (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu), about 11.9 g.

Corrosion
- Rusting of iron is electrochemical: anodic sites, Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻; cathodic sites, O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻ (neutral water). Fe²⁺ is then oxidised further to hydrated iron(III) oxide.
- Protection: coatings (paint, galvanising with zinc), sacrificial anodes of a more reactive metal (zinc or magnesium on ships and pipelines), impressed-current cathodic protection, and choosing compatible metals to avoid galvanic corrosion.

Exam tips: always use reduction potentials and subtract anode from cathode, check that n matches the balanced equation, and state which electrode is which.

Transition metals underpin many industrial catalysts and process materials. Their chemistry is dominated by partly filled d orbitals.

What makes a transition metal
- A d-block element that forms at least one stable ion with a partly filled d subshell. On this definition, Sc (Sc³⁺ is d⁰) and Zn (Zn²⁺ is d¹⁰) are often excluded.
- Characteristic properties: variable oxidation states, coloured compounds, complex formation, catalytic activity and (often) paramagnetism.

Complexes
- A complex has a central metal atom or ion bonded to ligands by dative (coordinate) bonds: each ligand donates an electron pair, so ligands are Lewis bases.
- Coordination number = number of dative bonds to the metal. Common geometries: 6 is octahedral ([Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺); 4 can be tetrahedral ([CoCl₄]²⁻) or square planar (d⁸ ions such as Ni²⁺ in [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ and Pt²⁺); 2 is linear ([Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺).
- Denticity: monodentate (H₂O, NH₃, Cl⁻, CN⁻), bidentate (ethane-1,2-diamine, "en"; ethanedioate), hexadentate (EDTA⁴⁻).
- Chelate effect: replacing monodentate ligands by a multidentate one increases the number of free particles, so entropy rises and the chelate complex is more stable. This is why EDTA is used to sequester metal ions in water treatment.
- Oxidation state in a complex: in [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃, NH₃ is neutral and there are three Cl⁻ counter-ions, so cobalt is +3.

Crystal field theory (octahedral)
- Ligands approaching along the axes raise the energy of the d orbitals pointing at them (e_g: d_z², d_x²−y²) more than those between the axes (t₂g: d_xy, d_xz, d_yz). The gap is Δ_o.
- Spectrochemical series (increasing Δ): I⁻ < Br⁻ < Cl⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < H₂O < NH₃ < en < CN⁻ < CO.
- High-spin vs low-spin: for d⁴–d⁷ ions, weak-field ligands give high-spin (electrons spread out), strong-field ligands give low-spin (electrons pair in t₂g). [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (d⁶) is high-spin with 4 unpaired electrons; [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ is low-spin with none.
- Spin-only magnetic moment μ = √(n(n + 2)) Bohr magnetons for n unpaired electrons: 4 unpaired gives about 4.9 BM.

Colour
- Complexes absorb visible light to promote electrons from t₂g to e_g; we see the complementary colour. [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ absorbs in the red/orange region and appears blue.
- d⁰ and d¹⁰ ions (Sc³⁺, Zn²⁺) have no d–d transitions and are usually colourless.
- Changing the ligand, oxidation state or coordination number changes Δ and so the colour.

Industrial catalysis (examples)
- Iron in the Haber–Bosch ammonia process.
- Vanadium(V) oxide in the contact process (SO₂ to SO₃ for sulfuric acid).
- Nickel in steam reforming of methane and in hydrogenation of vegetable oils.
- Platinum, palladium and rhodium in vehicle catalytic converters.
Heterogeneous catalysts work by adsorbing reactants on the surface, weakening bonds and then desorbing products; variable oxidation states also let homogeneous transition-metal catalysts take part in redox cycles.

Exam tips: work out the metal's oxidation state and d-electron count first, then decide geometry, spin state and number of unpaired electrons.

notes.h: Organic structure: functional groups, naming and isomerism
notes.body:
Most chemical-industry feedstocks and products are organic, so chemical engineers need to recognise structures, name them and understand how isomers can differ in properties.

Representing molecules
- Molecular formula (C₂H₆O), structural formula (CH₃CH₂OH), displayed formula (all bonds shown) and skeletal formula (carbon chain as zigzag lines; H on carbon not shown).
- Degree of unsaturation (rings plus π bonds) = (2C + 2 + N − H − X)/2. Benzene, C₆H₆, gives 4 (one ring plus three C=C).

Main functional groups
- Alkane (C–C only), alkene (C=C), alkyne (C≡C), arene (benzene ring).
- Haloalkane (C–X), alcohol (–OH), ether (C–O–C).
- Aldehyde (–CHO), ketone (C=O within the chain).
- Carboxylic acid (–COOH), ester (–COO–), amide (–CONH₂), acid chloride (–COCl).
- Amine (–NH₂), nitrile (–C≡N).

IUPAC naming essentials
- Find the longest chain containing the main functional group; number to give that group the lowest locant.
- Prefix for substituents (methyl-, chloro-), stem for chain length (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex-), suffix for the main group (-ol, -al, -one, -oic acid).
- Examples: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ is propan-2-ol; CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ is ethyl ethanoate.

Alcohols: primary, secondary, tertiary
- Classified by the number of carbons attached to the C bearing –OH.
- With acidified dichromate (orange to green): primary alcohols oxidise to aldehydes and then carboxylic acids; secondary to ketones; tertiary are not readily oxidised.

Isomerism
- Structural isomers: same molecular formula, different connectivity.
  - Chain isomers: butane and 2-methylpropane (C₄H₁₀ has 2 isomers; C₅H₁₂ has 3).
  - Position isomers: propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol.
  - Functional group isomers: ethanol and methoxymethane (C₂H₆O).
- Stereoisomers: same connectivity, different arrangement in space.
  - E/Z (geometric) isomerism needs restricted rotation (C=C) and two different groups on each carbon of the double bond. Priority by Cahn–Ingold–Prelog rules (higher atomic number wins); Z = higher priorities on the same side, E = opposite sides.
  - Optical isomerism: a carbon with four different groups (a stereocentre) gives a pair of non-superimposable mirror images (enantiomers), labelled R and S. Enantiomers have identical physical properties except that they rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions, and they can react differently with other chiral molecules (e.g. enzymes). A 50 : 50 mixture is a racemate and is optically inactive.

Why it matters
Isomers can have very different boiling points (affecting distillation), reactivities and biological effects, so a process often has to make one isomer selectively or separate it.

Exam tips: always draw the structure before naming, and for stereochemistry state the priorities you assigned.

A mechanism shows how bonds break and form, step by step, using curly arrows. Mechanisms explain which product forms, how fast and under what conditions, which is what matters when choosing reactor conditions.

Key ideas
- Curly arrows show movement of an electron pair, from a bond or lone pair to an atom or new bond. Half-headed (fish-hook) arrows show single electrons in radical reactions.
- Bond breaking: homolytic (one electron to each fragment, giving radicals) or heterolytic (both electrons to one fragment, giving ions).
- Nucleophile: electron-pair donor attracted to δ+ centres (OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃, H₂O).
- Electrophile: electron-pair acceptor attracted to electron-rich regions (H⁺, Br⁺ from polarised Br₂, NO₂⁺).
- Carbocation stability: tertiary > secondary > primary, because alkyl groups donate electron density (inductive effect and hyperconjugation).

Free-radical substitution (alkanes)
CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl under UV light:
- Initiation: Cl₂ → 2Cl•
- Propagation: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + •CH₃, then •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•
- Termination: any two radicals combine (e.g. 2•CH₃ → C₂H₆).
Further substitution gives a mixture (CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CCl₄), so selectivity is poor.

Electrophilic addition (alkenes)
- The π electrons attack an electrophile. HBr with propene: H⁺ adds to the end carbon to form the more stable secondary carbocation, then Br⁻ adds, giving mainly 2-bromopropane (Markovnikov's rule).
- With peroxides, HBr adds by a radical route, giving mainly 1-bromopropane (anti-Markovnikov).
- Bromine water is decolourised by alkenes: a simple test for C=C.

Nucleophilic substitution (haloalkanes)
- SN2: one step; the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving group, with inversion of configuration. Rate = k[RX][Nu⁻]. Favoured by primary substrates (little steric hindrance) and polar aprotic solvents.
- SN1: two steps; the leaving group departs to form a carbocation (rate-determining), then the nucleophile attacks either face, giving largely racemic product. Rate = k[RX]. Favoured by tertiary substrates and polar protic solvents.

Elimination
- Strong, bulky bases and higher temperatures favour elimination (E2 or E1) over substitution, giving alkenes. E2 needs the H and the leaving group anti-periplanar and usually gives the more substituted alkene (Zaitsev's rule), although very bulky bases can favour the less substituted one.

Electrophilic substitution (arenes)
Benzene's delocalised π system makes addition unfavourable because it would lose aromatic stability. Instead it undergoes substitution. Nitration: concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ form the nitronium ion NO₂⁺, which attacks the ring; loss of H⁺ restores aromaticity, giving nitrobenzene.

Carbonyl reactions
- Nucleophilic addition to aldehydes and ketones (e.g. cyanide, giving hydroxynitriles).
- Esterification: carboxylic acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water, acid-catalysed and reversible, so excess reagent or water removal drives conversion; a direct link to reactor and separation design.

Polymerisation
- Addition polymers (poly(ethene), PVC) form from alkenes with no by-product.
- Condensation polymers (polyesters, polyamides such as nylon) release a small molecule, usually water, at each link.

Exam tips: start arrows from a bond or lone pair, show charges and lone pairs, and justify which product dominates (carbocation stability, sterics, conditions).

cards.b: n (shell), l (subshell shape: s, p, d, f), m_l (orbital orientation, −l to +l), m_s (spin, ±½).
No two electrons in an atom can have the same four quantum numbers, so an orbital holds at most two electrons, of opposite spin.
Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing up.

cards.f: Electron configuration of Cr and Cu
cards.b: Cr: [Ar]3d⁵4s¹. Cu: [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ (exceptions to simple Aufbau filling).
[Ar]3d⁶: the two 4s electrons are lost first.

cards.f: Why first IE of O is lower than N
cards.b: O's fourth 2p electron is paired in an orbital, and the extra electron–electron repulsion makes it easier to remove.
Eₙ = −13.6 eV/n²; the n = 2 → 1 transition emits 10.2 eV (about 122 nm).
Fluorine, about 4.0 on the Pauling scale.
Electron pairs around a central atom repel and arrange to be as far apart as possible; lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs.
Trigonal pyramidal, about 107° (four electron pairs, one lone pair).
Bent, about 104.5° (four electron pairs, two lone pairs).
Its two polar C=O bonds point in opposite directions in a linear molecule, so the dipoles cancel.
H covalently bonded to N, O or F, interacting with a lone pair on another N, O or F atom.

cards.f: σ and π bonds in a C=C double bond
cards.b: One σ bond (end-on overlap) and one π bond (sideways overlap of p orbitals); the π bond prevents rotation.
ΔH ≈ Σ(bond enthalpies broken) − Σ(bond enthalpies formed); approximate because mean values are averages.
Octahedral, 90° bond angles (six bonding pairs, no lone pairs).
The reactant that would be used up first if the reaction went to completion; it sets the maximum amount of product.
Moles of a reactant that react divided by moles of that reactant fed.
(Amount fed − amount stoichiometrically needed for the limiting reactant)/(amount needed) × 100.
Moles of desired product formed ÷ moles that would form if all the limiting reactant reacted with no side reactions.
The air containing exactly the O₂ needed for complete combustion of the fuel (air ≈ 21% O₂, 79% N₂ by moles).
Wet basis includes water vapour in the total; dry basis composition excludes it.

cards.f: Molar volume of an ideal gas
cards.b: About 22.4 L/mol at 0 °C and 1 atm; about 24.8 L/mol at 25 °C and 1 bar.
ξ defined by nᵢ = nᵢ,₀ + νᵢξ for each species, with νᵢ negative for reactants.
Acid: proton donor. Base: proton acceptor. Each acid has a conjugate base differing by one H⁺.
An electron-pair acceptor (e.g. BF₃, AlCl₃).
Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴, so pH + pOH = 14.
[H₃O⁺] ≈ √(Ka c), valid when ionisation is small (a few per cent or less).
pH = pKa + log₁₀([A⁻]/[HA]).

cards.f: pH at half-equivalence (weak acid + strong base)
cards.b: pH = pKa, because [HA] = [A⁻].
No. Its pH is below 7 because Kw is larger, but [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻], so it is neutral.

cards.f: Relationship between Ka and Kb of a conjugate pair
cards.b: Ka × Kb = Kw, so pKa + pKb = 14 at 25 °C.
Oxidation is loss of electrons (oxidation state rises); reduction is gain of electrons (oxidation state falls).

cards.f: Oxidation state of Mn in MnO₄⁻

cards.b: E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode), using standard reduction potentials.
ΔG° = −nFE°cell; a positive E°cell means ΔG° < 0 (spontaneous under standard conditions).
E = E° − (0.0592/n) log₁₀ Q.
Charge Q = It; moles of electrons = Q/F with F = 96 485 C/mol.
Anode: oxidation (negative in a galvanic cell, positive in electrolysis). Cathode: reduction.
A more reactive metal (e.g. Zn or Mg) connected to steel corrodes in preference, protecting the steel.
A molecule or ion that donates a lone pair to a metal to form a dative (coordinate) bond; a Lewis base.
The number of dative bonds from ligands to the central metal ion.
Multidentate ligands form more stable complexes than equivalent monodentate ones, mainly due to an increase in entropy.

cards.f: t₂g and e_g in an octahedral field
cards.b: e_g (d_z², d_x²−y²) point at ligands and are raised; t₂g (d_xy, d_xz, d_yz) lie between axes and are lower. Gap = Δ_o.
Strong-field ligands (large Δ) cause pairing in t₂g (low-spin); weak-field ligands give maximum unpaired electrons (high-spin).
μ = √(n(n + 2)) BM for n unpaired electrons (e.g. n = 4 gives about 4.9 BM).

cards.f: Why Zn²⁺ compounds are usually colourless
cards.b: Zn²⁺ is d¹⁰: the d subshell is full, so no d–d transitions are possible.
Vanadium(V) oxide, V₂O₅, for oxidising SO₂ to SO₃.
(2C + 2 + N − H − X)/2 = number of rings plus π bonds.
Compounds with the same molecular formula but different atom connectivity (chain, position or functional group isomers).
Restricted rotation (usually C=C) and two different groups on each carbon of the double bond.
A carbon atom bonded to four different groups; gives rise to a pair of enantiomers.
A 50 : 50 mixture of two enantiomers; optically inactive because the rotations cancel.
Gives a ketone with acidified dichromate (orange → green); no further oxidation under normal conditions.

cards.f: Number of structural isomers of C₅H₁₂
cards.b: Three: pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane.
Higher atomic number of the directly attached atom gets higher priority; if tied, compare the next atoms out.
An electron-pair donor that attacks electron-poor (δ+) centres, e.g. OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃.
An electron-pair acceptor that attacks electron-rich regions, e.g. H⁺, NO₂⁺, polarised Br₂.
One step, backside attack, inversion of configuration, rate = k[RX][Nu⁻], favoured for primary haloalkanes.
Two steps via a carbocation, rate = k[RX], largely racemic product, favoured for tertiary haloalkanes.
H adds to the carbon with more H atoms, via the more stable carbocation, so X ends up on the more substituted carbon.
Tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl, because alkyl groups stabilise the positive charge.
The nitronium ion NO₂⁺, formed from concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄.

cards.f: Why benzene favours substitution over addition
cards.b: Substitution keeps the delocalised aromatic π system, which is especially stable; addition would destroy it.

questions.q: Which is the correct ground-state electron configuration of the Fe³⁺ ion?
questions.why: Fe is [Ar]3d⁶4s². On ionisation the 4s electrons go first, then one 3d electron, leaving [Ar]3d⁵. [Ar]3d³4s² wrongly removes 3d electrons while keeping 4s. [Ar]3d⁶4s² is neutral iron. [Ar]3d⁴4s¹ has the right electron count (23) but the wrong arrangement, keeping a 4s electron that should be removed first.

questions.q: Why is the first ionisation energy of boron lower than that of beryllium?
options: Boron's outer electron is in a 2p orbital, which is higher in energy and partly shielded by the 2s electrons
Boron has a smaller nuclear charge than beryllium
Boron's outer electron is paired in an orbital
Boron's outer electron is in the third shell
questions.why: B's outermost electron is in 2p, which is higher in energy than 2s and slightly shielded by the 2s pair, so it is easier to remove. B has a larger nuclear charge (5) than Be (4), not smaller. Pairing explains the N to O dip, not Be to B, since B has a single 2p electron. Both elements use only shells 1 and 2.

questions.q: Explain the general trend in first ionisation energy across period 3 (Na to Ar) and account for the two exceptions.
markScheme: General increase across the period due to rising nuclear charge/Z_eff with similar shielding and decreasing radius
Al lower than Mg: outer electron in 3p, higher energy and shielded by 3s
S lower than P: paired 3p electron experiences extra repulsion
Use of correct terms (shielding, effective nuclear charge)
questions.modelAnswer: Across period 3 the nuclear charge rises by one each step while the electrons being removed are in the same shell, so shielding hardly changes; effective nuclear charge increases and atomic radius falls, making electrons harder to remove. So first ionisation energy generally rises from Na to Ar. Aluminium is lower than magnesium because its outermost electron is in a 3p orbital, higher in energy than 3s and partly shielded by the 3s pair. Sulfur is lower than phosphorus because sulfur's fourth 3p electron must pair in an orbital already holding one electron, and the repulsion between the paired electrons makes it easier to remove.

questions.q: What is the shape of the NH₃ molecule?
questions.why: N has three bonding pairs and one lone pair; the electron pairs are tetrahedral but the atoms form a trigonal pyramid. Trigonal planar would need only three electron pairs, as in BF₃. Tetrahedral describes the arrangement of electron pairs, not the shape of the atoms, and would need four bonded atoms. Bent applies to two bonded atoms with two lone pairs, as in H₂O.

questions.q: Why does water (Mr 18) boil at a much higher temperature than hydrogen sulfide (Mr 34)?
options: The O–H covalent bond is broken on boiling
Water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other
Water has stronger London forces because it has more electrons
questions.why: O is small and highly electronegative, so water forms strong hydrogen bonds; S is less electronegative and H₂S has only weaker dipole–dipole and London forces. H₂S actually has more electrons (18 versus 10), so its London forces are stronger, not weaker. Boiling separates molecules; no covalent bonds are broken. H₂S is bent and slightly polar, so calling it non-polar is wrong.

questions.q: Use mean bond enthalpies (C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O in CO₂ 805, O–H 464 kJ/mol) to estimate ΔH for CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g). Explain why the answer differs from the measured value of about −802 kJ/mol.
markScheme: Bonds broken: 4 C–H + 2 O=O = 1652 + 996 = 2648 kJ/mol
Bonds formed: 2 C=O + 4 O–H = 1610 + 1856 = 3466 kJ/mol
Mean bond enthalpies are averages over many compounds, so they are not exact for these molecules
Method only valid for all-gaseous species
questions.modelAnswer: Bonds broken: four C–H bonds (4 × 413 = 1652 kJ/mol) and two O=O bonds (2 × 498 = 996 kJ/mol), a total of 2648 kJ/mol. Bonds formed: two C=O bonds in CO₂ (2 × 805 = 1610 kJ/mol) and four O–H bonds (4 × 464 = 1856 kJ/mol), a total of 3466 kJ/mol. So ΔH ≈ 2648 − 3466 = −818 kJ/mol. The measured value differs because mean bond enthalpies are averages taken over many different molecules, so the actual strength of a bond in CH₄ or H₂O differs slightly from the average. The method also only applies when all species are gases.

questions.q: 28 kg of N₂ and 8 kg of H₂ are fed to an ammonia reactor (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃). Which statement is correct?
options: H₂ is limiting and the maximum NH₃ is about 45 kg
N₂ is limiting and the maximum NH₃ is about 17 kg
N₂ is limiting and the maximum NH₃ is about 34 kg
H₂ is limiting because its mass is smaller
questions.why: N₂ = 28/28.0 = 1.00 kmol, needing 3.00 kmol H₂; 8 kg H₂ is about 3.97 kmol, so H₂ is in excess and N₂ is limiting. 2 kmol NH₃ × 17.0 kg/kmol ≈ 34 kg. Comparing masses rather than moles wrongly makes H₂ look limiting. About 45 kg would need all the H₂ to react (3.97 × ⅔ × 17.0), which the N₂ cannot support. About 17 kg forgets the 1 : 2 ratio of N₂ to NH₃.

questions.q: A compound contains 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O by mass, and its molar mass is 180 g/mol. What is its molecular formula?
questions.why: Mole ratio C : H : O = 40.0/12.0 : 6.7/1.0 : 53.3/16.0 ≈ 3.33 : 6.7 : 3.33 = 1 : 2 : 1, so the empirical formula CH₂O (30 g/mol). 180/30 = 6, giving C₆H₁₂O₆. CH₂O is only the empirical formula. C₃H₆O₃ has a molar mass of 90 g/mol. C₆H₆O₆ has the wrong H : C ratio for these percentages.

questions.q: In a reactor, 100 mol/s of ethylene is fed with water to make ethanol (C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH). 60 mol/s of ethylene reacts: 54 mol/s forms ethanol and the rest forms diethyl ether by 2C₂H₄ + H₂O → (C₂H₅)₂O. Calculate the fractional conversion of ethylene, the ethanol yield and the selectivity of ethanol relative to ether.
markScheme: Conversion = 60/100 = 0.60
Ethylene to ether = 6 mol/s, so ether formed = 3 mol/s
Yield of ethanol = 54/100 = 0.54 (based on ethylene fed)
Selectivity = 54/3 = 18 mol ethanol per mol ether
States the definitions used
questions.modelAnswer: Fractional conversion of ethylene = 60/100 = 0.60. Of the 60 mol/s reacted, 54 mol/s gives ethanol and 6 mol/s goes to ether; since two ethylene molecules form one ether molecule, 3 mol/s of ether is formed. Taking yield as moles of ethanol formed per mole of ethylene fed (the maximum being 1 mol ethanol per mol ethylene), the yield is 54/100 = 0.54; on the basis of ethylene consumed it would be 54/60 = 0.90. Selectivity, defined as moles of desired product per mole of undesired product, is 54/3 = 18.

questions.q: What is the approximate pH of 0.10 M ethanoic acid (pKa 4.76)?
questions.why: [H₃O⁺] ≈ √(Ka c) = √(1.74 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.10) ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻³ M, so pH ≈ 2.9. pH 1.0 assumes complete ionisation, as for a strong acid. pH 4.8 is the pKa, which is the pH of an equimolar buffer, not of the acid alone. pH 5.8 comes from adding pKa and the concentration term instead of halving their sum.

questions.q: A buffer contains 0.10 M ethanoic acid (pKa 4.76) and 0.20 M sodium ethanoate. What is its pH?
questions.why: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]) = 4.76 + log 2 ≈ 5.06. About 4.46 inverts the ratio ([HA]/[A⁻]). About 4.76 would be correct only if the acid and salt concentrations were equal. pH 7 ignores the buffer chemistry altogether.

questions.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 M ethanoic acid (pKa 4.76) is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH. Find the pH (a) at the start, (b) after 12.5 cm³ of NaOH, and (c) explain why the equivalence point is above pH 7 and choose a suitable indicator.
markScheme: (a) pH ≈ ½(pKa − log c) ≈ 2.88
(b) Half-equivalence: [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa = 4.76
(c) At equivalence the solution contains ethanoate ions, a weak base that hydrolyses to give OH⁻
Equivalence pH > 7 (about 8.7 here)
Indicator: phenolphthalein (changes about pH 8.2–10)
questions.modelAnswer: (a) For the acid alone, [H₃O⁺] ≈ √(Ka c) = √(1.74 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.100) ≈ 1.32 × 10⁻³ M, so pH ≈ 2.88. (b) 12.5 cm³ of NaOH neutralises half the acid, so [HA] = [A⁻] and, by Henderson–Hasselbalch, pH = pKa = 4.76. (c) At equivalence all the acid has become sodium ethanoate (0.0500 M in 50 cm³). Ethanoate is the conjugate base of a weak acid and reacts with water, CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻, so the solution is basic; with Kb = Kw/Ka ≈ 5.8 × 10⁻¹⁰, [OH⁻] ≈ √(Kb × 0.05) ≈ 5.4 × 10⁻⁶ M, giving pH ≈ 8.7. Phenolphthalein, which changes colour at about pH 8.2–10, sits on the steep part of the curve, so it is suitable.

questions.q: Using E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V and E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V, what is ΔG° for Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu (F = 96 485 C/mol)?
questions.why: E°cell = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V and n = 2, so ΔG° = −2 × 96 485 × 1.10 ≈ −212 kJ/mol. About −106 kJ/mol uses n = 1. A positive value has the wrong sign; the reaction is spontaneous. About −81 kJ/mol comes from wrongly adding the potentials as 0.34 + (−0.76) = −0.42 V and then dropping the sign.

questions.q: A current of 10 A is passed through copper(II) sulfate solution for 1 hour. What mass of copper is deposited at the cathode (Cu = 63.5 g/mol)?
questions.why: Q = 10 × 3600 = 36 000 C, which is 36 000/96 485 = 0.373 mol of electrons; Cu²⁺ needs 2 electrons, so 0.187 mol Cu ≈ 11.9 g. About 23.7 g forgets that two electrons are needed per copper atom. About 0.20 g uses 60 seconds instead of 3600. About 5.9 g divides by 4 instead of 2.

questions.q: A Daniell cell is set up with [Zn²⁺] = 1.0 M and [Cu²⁺] = 0.010 M at 298 K. Write the cell reaction, identify the anode, and calculate the cell potential. Explain why it differs from 1.10 V.
markScheme: Cell reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu; anode is zinc (oxidation)
Lower because lower [Cu²⁺] makes the reduction less favourable (Le Chatelier/Q > 1)
questions.modelAnswer: The cell reaction is Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s). Zinc is oxidised, so the zinc electrode is the anode (the negative terminal). E° = E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) − E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V. The reaction quotient is Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] = 1.0/0.010 = 100 (solids omitted). By the Nernst equation, E = 1.10 − (0.0592/2) log₁₀ 100 = 1.10 − 0.0592 ≈ 1.04 V. The potential is lower than standard because the reactant Cu²⁺ is dilute, so the driving force for its reduction is smaller (Q > 1).

questions.q: What is the oxidation state of cobalt in [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃?
questions.why: NH₃ is a neutral ligand, and three Cl⁻ counter-ions balance the complex, so the complex ion is [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ and cobalt is +3. +6 confuses the coordination number (six NH₃ ligands) with the oxidation state. 0 ignores the chloride counter-ions. +2 assumes cobalt's most familiar aqueous oxidation state (as in [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺) instead of working it out from the formula, which needs a 3+ complex ion to balance three chloride ions.

questions.q: How many unpaired electrons does the low-spin octahedral complex [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ have?
questions.why: Fe is +2 here (6 × CN⁻ = −6, overall −4), so Fe²⁺ is d⁶. Cyanide is a strong-field ligand, so all six electrons pair in the t₂g set, leaving none unpaired. Four unpaired electrons would describe a high-spin d⁶ ion, such as [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺. Two unpaired electrons does not fit d⁶ in either spin state in an octahedral field. Six would mean every d electron unpaired, which is impossible with five d orbitals.

questions.q: Explain why [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is coloured while [Zn(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is colourless, and why adding excess ammonia to the copper solution changes its colour.
markScheme: Cu²⁺ is d⁹: a partly filled d subshell allows d–d transitions (t₂g → e_g) that absorb visible light
Observed colour is the complementary colour (blue for Cu aqua ion)
Zn²⁺ is d¹⁰: full d subshell, no d–d transitions, so no visible absorption
NH₃ substitutes for water, giving a different ligand with larger Δ, so the absorbed wavelength and colour change (deep blue)
questions.modelAnswer: Cu²⁺ has a d⁹ configuration. In the octahedral aqua complex the d orbitals are split, and an electron can be promoted from the lower t₂g level to the partly empty e_g level by absorbing visible light (mainly in the red/orange region), so the solution looks blue, the complementary colour. Zn²⁺ is d¹⁰: both sets of d orbitals are full, so no d–d transition is possible and no visible light is absorbed. Adding excess ammonia replaces some water ligands (forming [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺). Ammonia is higher in the spectrochemical series, so the splitting is larger and the absorption moves to shorter wavelengths, making the solution a deeper, more intense blue.

questions.q: Which compound can show E/Z isomerism?
questions.why: In but-2-ene each double-bond carbon carries one H and one CH₃, so E and Z forms exist. In but-1-ene one carbon of the double bond carries two H atoms. In 2-methylpropene one carbon carries two CH₃ groups (and the other two H atoms). Ethene has two H atoms on each carbon. In all three cases swapping groups gives the same molecule, so there is no E/Z isomerism.

questions.q: Propan-2-ol is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate. What is the organic product?
options: No reaction, because it is a tertiary alcohol
questions.why: Propan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol, which is oxidised to the ketone propanone. Propanal and propanoic acid come from the primary alcohol propan-1-ol. Propan-2-ol is secondary, not tertiary (the C–OH carbon has two carbon neighbours), so it does react.

questions.q: Draw or describe the structural isomers of C₄H₁₀O that are alcohols, classify each as primary, secondary or tertiary, and identify which one is chiral.
markScheme: Butan-1-ol (primary)
Butan-2-ol (secondary)
2-methylpropan-1-ol (primary) and 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tertiary)
Butan-2-ol is chiral: C2 bears H, OH, CH₃ and C₂H₅
questions.modelAnswer: There are four alcohol isomers of C₄H₁₀O. Butan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH, is primary. Butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, is secondary. 2-methylpropan-1-ol, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH, is primary. 2-methylpropan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃COH, is tertiary. Only butan-2-ol is chiral: its second carbon carries four different groups (H, OH, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃), so it exists as a pair of enantiomers.

questions.q: What is the major product when HBr adds to propene (no peroxides present)?
questions.why: H⁺ adds to the terminal CH₂ to give the more stable secondary carbocation, which Br⁻ then attacks, giving 2-bromopropane (Markovnikov). 1-bromopropane is the major product only by the radical route when peroxides are present. 1,2-dibromopropane comes from adding Br₂, not HBr. Propan-2-ol would need water as the nucleophile (acid-catalysed hydration).

questions.q: The rate of a substitution reaction doubles when the concentration of hydroxide ions is doubled, and the product from a chiral haloalkane shows inverted configuration. Which mechanism fits?
questions.why: First order in nucleophile and inversion of configuration both point to a single-step backside attack, SN2. SN1 has a rate independent of [OH⁻] and gives a largely racemic product. E1 is an elimination giving an alkene, not a substitution product, and its rate also does not depend on the base. Free-radical substitution involves radicals, not hydroxide ions, and does not produce stereospecific inversion.

questions.q: Describe the mechanism of the reaction between methane and chlorine in ultraviolet light, and explain why it is a poor way to make pure chloromethane.
markScheme: Initiation: Cl₂ → 2Cl• by homolytic fission using UV
Propagation step 1: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + •CH₃
Propagation step 2: •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl• (chain continues)
Termination: two radicals combine, e.g. •CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl or 2•CH₃ → C₂H₆
Poor selectivity: further substitution gives CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CCl₄ and C₂H₆ by-products, needing separation
questions.modelAnswer: Ultraviolet light supplies the energy to break the Cl–Cl bond homolytically: Cl₂ → 2Cl• (initiation). In propagation, a chlorine radical abstracts a hydrogen atom: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + •CH₃; the methyl radical then reacts with Cl₂: •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•, regenerating Cl• so the chain continues. Termination occurs when two radicals meet, for example Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂, •CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl or 2•CH₃ → C₂H₆. The method gives poor selectivity because Cl• can also abstract H from chloromethane, leading to CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄, and termination produces ethane, so the product is a mixture that must be separated, for example by distillation.

questions.q: A fuel gas containing 80 mol% CH₄, 15 mol% C₂H₆ and 5 mol% N₂ is fed to a furnace at 100 mol/s and burned completely with 20% excess air (air: 21 mol% O₂, 79 mol% N₂). (a) Write balanced combustion equations for methane and ethane. [3] (b) Calculate the theoretical O₂, the O₂ supplied and the air feed rate. [5] (c) Calculate the molar flow of each component in the flue gas and its composition on a wet basis. [8] (d) Give the composition on a dry basis and explain why flue-gas analysers often report dry compositions. [4]
markScheme: (a) CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O; C₂H₆ + 3.5O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O (or 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O)
(b) Theoretical O₂ = 2(80) + 3.5(15) = 212.5 mol/s; supplied = 1.2 × 212.5 = 255 mol/s
(b) Air = 255/0.21 ≈ 1214 mol/s, containing ≈ 959 mol/s N₂
(c) Total ≈ 1322 mol/s; wet composition CO₂ 8.3%, H₂O 15.5%, O₂ 3.2%, N₂ 73.0%
(d) Dry total ≈ 1117 mol/s: CO₂ 9.9%, O₂ 3.8%, N₂ 86.3%
(d) Water condenses in sampling lines/analysers, so samples are dried before measurement
questions.modelAnswer:
Basis: 100 mol/s fuel gas, so 80 mol/s CH₄, 15 mol/s C₂H₆ and 5 mol/s N₂.

(a) CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
C₂H₆ + 3.5O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O (equivalently 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O).

(b) Theoretical O₂ = 2 × 80 + 3.5 × 15 = 160 + 52.5 = 212.5 mol/s.
With 20% excess, O₂ supplied = 1.2 × 212.5 = 255 mol/s.
Air feed = 255/0.21 ≈ 1214.3 mol/s, of which N₂ = 0.79 × 1214.3 ≈ 959.3 mol/s.

(c) Complete combustion, so no fuel or CO remains.
CO₂: 80 (from CH₄) + 2 × 15 (from C₂H₆) = 110 mol/s
H₂O: 2 × 80 + 3 × 15 = 160 + 45 = 205 mol/s
O₂ (unreacted excess): 255 − 212.5 = 42.5 mol/s
N₂: 959.3 (from air) + 5 (from fuel) = 964.3 mol/s
Total = 110 + 205 + 42.5 + 964.3 ≈ 1321.8 mol/s
Wet-basis mole fractions:
CO₂ 110/1321.8 ≈ 8.3%
H₂O 205/1321.8 ≈ 15.5%
O₂ 42.5/1321.8 ≈ 3.2%
N₂ 964.3/1321.8 ≈ 73.0%
Check: the atom balances close. Carbon in: 80 + 30 = 110 = CO₂ out. Hydrogen in: 4 × 80 + 6 × 15 = 410 atoms = 2 × 205 in H₂O out.

(d) Removing water, the dry total is 1321.8 − 205 = 1116.8 mol/s:
CO₂ 110/1116.8 ≈ 9.9%
O₂ 42.5/1116.8 ≈ 3.8%
N₂ 964.3/1116.8 ≈ 86.3%
Flue-gas analysers usually cool and dry the sample, because water would condense in sampling lines and instruments, causing errors and damage. Reporting on a dry basis also makes the O₂ and CO₂ readings independent of the fuel's hydrogen content and humidity, so they can be used directly to check the excess air (here about 3.8% O₂ dry).

questions.q: (a) Balance the reaction between manganate(VII) ions and iron(II) ions in acidic solution, using half-equations. [4] (b) 25.0 cm³ of an iron(II) solution needs 22.50 cm³ of 0.0200 M KMnO₄ to reach the end point. Find the Fe²⁺ concentration. [4] (c) Using E°(MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺) = +1.51 V and E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +0.77 V, find E°cell and ΔG° for the reaction in (a), and comment on why no separate indicator is needed. [6] (d) Explain the electrochemistry of rusting of a steel pipeline in damp soil and describe two engineering methods of protecting it. [6]
markScheme: (a) MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O; Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻; overall MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O
(c) MnO₄⁻ is intensely purple and Mn²⁺ almost colourless: first excess gives a permanent pink (self-indicating)
(d) Anodic Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻; cathodic O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻; Fe(OH)₂ oxidised to hydrated Fe₂O₃ (rust)
(d) Protection: coatings/wrapping; sacrificial Mg or Zn anodes; impressed-current cathodic protection (any two, explained)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Reduction: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O (Mn goes from +7 to +2).
Oxidation: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻.
Multiply the iron half-equation by 5 and add:
MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O.
Check charge: left −1 + 10 + 8 = +17; right +2 + 15 = +17.

(b) n(MnO₄⁻) = 0.0200 mol/dm³ × 0.02250 dm³ = 4.50 × 10⁻⁴ mol.
From the 1 : 5 ratio, n(Fe²⁺) = 5 × 4.50 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.25 × 10⁻³ mol.
[Fe²⁺] = 2.25 × 10⁻³/0.0250 = 0.0900 mol/dm³.

(c) MnO₄⁻ is reduced (cathode) and Fe²⁺ oxidised (anode):
E°cell = 1.51 − 0.77 = 0.74 V.
Five electrons are transferred, so ΔG° = −nFE° = −5 × 96 485 × 0.74 ≈ −3.57 × 10⁵ J/mol ≈ −357 kJ/mol, strongly spontaneous.
No separate indicator is needed because MnO₄⁻ is intensely purple while Mn²⁺ is almost colourless at these concentrations. While Fe²⁺ remains, added MnO₄⁻ is decolourised immediately; the first slight excess gives a permanent pale pink colour, marking the end point.

(d) Rusting is an electrochemical cell on the steel surface, with the damp soil as electrolyte. At anodic regions iron is oxidised: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻. Electrons flow through the metal to cathodic regions, where dissolved oxygen is reduced: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. Fe²⁺ and OH⁻ form Fe(OH)₂, which is further oxidised by oxygen to hydrated iron(III) oxide, rust. Differences in oxygen supply, soil chemistry or metal composition set up the anodic and cathodic areas, so pitting can concentrate in poorly aerated zones.
Protection methods:
- Coatings and wrapping (e.g. epoxy or polymer coatings) separate steel from the electrolyte; they are usually combined with cathodic protection because coatings have defects.
- Sacrificial anodes: blocks of a more reactive metal such as magnesium or zinc are connected to the pipe. They have more negative electrode potentials, so they are oxidised instead of the iron, making the whole pipe a cathode. They must be replaced as they are consumed.
- Impressed-current cathodic protection: a DC power supply drives current from inert or semi-inert anodes through the soil to the pipe, holding the steel at a potential where it does not corrode; used for long pipelines where sacrificial anodes would be insufficient.
